subtype: Palm out as boundary in arguments [Regulating]
passage: In the small shop behind the tea stall, Tanuja's sister Zeenat was in full flow about the cricket match, then the neighbour, then the missing scissors. Tanuja had a exam paper to check. She raised her palm. "Give me a second." Zeenat stopped mid-word, mouth open. Tanuja closed her eyes, breathed, and said, "I'm not saying you're wrong. I just can't listen and think at once. Tell me in ten minutes?" Zeenat pressed her lips together. "Fine. But you didn't have to do the hand." "I know. Sorry. It was the words that mattered." She passed Zeenat a biscuit.

qa.q: What was Zeenat talking about when Tanuja raised her palm?
qa.a: Zeenat was talking about the cricket match, the neighbour and the missing scissors.

qa.q: What did Tanuja mean by raising her palm, and what was she feeling?
qa.a: She meant she needed a moment because she couldn't listen and think together. She felt overloaded, not angry at Zeenat.

qa.q: What could Tanuja do next time to keep respect intact?
qa.a: She can say a few words like "give me a second" as she raises her hand, and offer a time to talk later. That protects her boundary without sounding dismissive.

qa.q: How might Zeenat have felt when the palm went up?
qa.a: She felt cut off and a little dismissed, which is why she complained about the hand. Tanuja's explanation and apology eased it.

grounding: A teenager raises a palm to stop a sibling mid-rant, and adds words so the boundary stays respectful.

subtype: Palm out as boundary in arguments [Regulating]
passage: Kaito was halfway through a maths problem when Clara started her long rant about the school trip. He held up a palm without a word. Clara froze. "Seriously?" she said. "You're shutting me down?" Kaito took off his headphones. "No. Sorry. Give me a second, I lost my place." He finished the line, then turned around. "Okay. Go." Clara folded her arms, still stiff. "That hand looked like 'talk to the hand'." "I get that. I disagree with parts of your plan, though, and I wanted to listen properly." She sat on the desk edge. "Then listen properly."

qa.q: What was Kaito doing when Clara started her rant?
qa.a: He was halfway through a maths problem.

qa.q: What was Clara feeling when Kaito held up his palm?
qa.a: She felt shut down and dismissed, and her folded arms and stiff voice show it. Kaito's actual reason was that he needed a moment.

qa.q: What would you advise Kaito about using the palm?
qa.a: He can pair it with words like "give me a second" so it reads as a pause and not a brush-off. That keeps the respect.

qa.q: How does Kaito see the situation compared to Clara?
qa.a: He wanted to finish his thought so he could listen properly, and he disagrees with parts of her plan. She only saw the hand.

grounding: A teenager raises a palm mid-rant to say he needs a moment, and it can read as dismissive without words.

passage:
In the hostel room, Kavitha was pacing, ranting about their friend Meera skipping the group project meeting. "She's so selfish! She always does this! And she—"
Vasudha, sitting on her bed with her notes, raised a hand, palm out.
Kavitha stopped, eyebrows up. "Are you seriously shushing me?"
"No, no," Vasudha said quickly. "Give me a second. I need to think. I don't fully agree with you."
Kavitha folded her arms. "Go on."
"Meera told me her mother was in hospital this week. That's why she missed it."
Kavitha's shoulders dropped. "Oh. I didn't know."
"I'm not saying you're wrong to be annoyed. Just... maybe ask her first?"
Kavitha sat down on the bed. "Yeah. Okay."

qa.q: Why did Meera miss the group project meeting?
qa.a: Her mother was in hospital this week.

qa.q: What was Kavitha feeling when Vasudha raised a palm?
qa.a: Kavitha felt annoyed and a bit offended, thinking Vasudha was shushing her dismissively.

qa.q: What did Vasudha do that kept the boundary respectful?
qa.a: She added words like "Give me a second" and explained she disagreed, so the palm didn't feel like a put-down.

qa.q: How might Meera feel if she heard Kavitha's rant?
qa.a: Meera would probably feel hurt and misunderstood, since she was dealing with her mother being in hospital.

grounding: In a hostel room, a teenager raises a palm to pause a friend's rant and adds words to keep respect intact.

Hi Chaitanya,
I know I made you angry at dinner. When you started going on about my maths marks in front of Mummy and Papa, I raised my palm right in your face. You stopped, but you looked insulted and left the table.
I wasn't trying to dismiss you. I was already upset about the marks, and hearing it again made me want to cry at the table. The palm meant, "Stop, I can't take any more right now."
But I get it. A hand in the face without words looks rude.
Next time I'll say, "Give me a second, bhaiya." And maybe later you can help me with the chapter I messed up?
Ira

qa.a: Ira felt upset and close to tears about the marks, and needed Chaitanya to stop.

qa.a: Ira will say "Give me a second, bhaiya" instead of just raising a palm.

qa.q: How might Chaitanya have felt when Ira raised a palm in Chaitanya's face?
qa.a: Chaitanya probably felt insulted and dismissed, since the palm came without any words.

subtype: Palm out as boundary in arguments [Regulating]
passage:
"Jahnavi, you asked for the school magazine what I learned in debate club. Okay, here's one thing.
In practice, when the other side gets loud, I used to just raise my palm, like this, to stop them. My coach said it looked dismissive, like I didn't care what they said.
So now, when I want a pause or I don't agree, I raise my palm but I also say, 'Give me a second,' or 'Can I respond to that?' It works better. People stop, but they don't feel shut down.
Last week, the other team's captain even thanked me after the round. She said I was the only one who didn't make her feel stupid.
So yes, I, Irfan, am still a hand-raiser. Just a polite one now."

qa.q: What did Irfan's coach say the raised palm looked like?
qa.a: Dismissive, like Irfan didn't care what they said.

qa.q: How did the other team's captain feel about Irfan's polite palm?
qa.a: She felt respected and grateful, thanking Irfan for not making her feel stupid.

qa.q: What did Irfan learn to do with the raised palm?
qa.a: Irfan learned to add a few words like "Give me a second" so the palm protected a boundary without shutting people down.

qa.q: How might the other side in debate see a raised palm without words?
qa.a: They might feel dismissed and shut down, as if their points didn't matter.

grounding: A teenager explains in an interview how a raised palm in debate can protect a boundary, and words keep respect intact.

subtype: Palm out as boundary in arguments [Regulating]
passage: I'm Maria, their cousin, and I was staying with them for Onam when it happened. Irawati was in the middle of a rant at Joseph about him using her charger again, hands flying, voice climbing. Joseph suddenly put his palm up, flat, right in front of her face. Irawati stopped, but her eyes went narrow. "Did you just palm me? Like I'm a dog?" I couldn't tell what Joseph meant; he just stood there with his hand up. Then he lowered it and said, "Sorry. I meant give me a second. You're right about the charger. I just couldn't think with the shouting." Irawati was still annoyed, but her shoulders came down. "Then say that, not the hand." He nodded, handed her the charger, and said, "Give me a second, please." They both laughed.

qa.q: What had Joseph been using again?
qa.a: Irawati's charger.

qa.q: What was Irawati feeling when her eyes went narrow?
qa.a: Irawati felt insulted and dismissed, reading the flat palm as being shut up rudely.

qa.q: What kept the respect intact after the palm?
qa.a: Joseph lowered his hand, apologised, agreed about the charger and put his need into words: 'Give me a second.'

qa.q: How did Joseph see his own raised palm?
qa.a: To Joseph it meant 'give me a second': he needed a pause to think through the shouting, not to dismiss Irawati.

grounding: It shows a teenager raising a palm to pause a sibling's rant, the gesture reading as dismissive, and a few words restoring respect, as seen by a cousin.
